title: Integrability and non-integrability of the functions of the second kind with respect to the N-extremal measures
author: Christian Berg and Ryszard Szwarc
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: original Proposition 3.1 of the article (source label thm:1-2, source0.tex lines 355--363), which the article states to be new and which is the technical input of its main theorem: for every N-extremal measure $\mu$ the functions $p(u)B(u,v)$ and $p(u)D(u,v)$ are $\mu$-integrable with vanishing integrals, the function $B(u,\cdot)$ lies in $L^2(\mu)$ only for the one N-extremal measure supported by its zero set and is the zero element there, and the same holds for $D$ with the measure $\mu[v_0]$. It is delivered with the author's own complete 17-line proof at source0.tex lines 365--381. H2: the proof must be reconstructed rather than quoted. The solver has to express $pB$ and $pD$ through the Cauchy transforms $F_{(q_k(v))}$ and $F_{(p_k(v))}$ of $\eqref{eq:FGc}$, use Cauchy--Schwarz to get $L^1(\mu)$ convergence of the polynomial approximants, invoke the vanishing integrals of Proposition 2.1 for $n>\deg p$ to pass to the limit, and then run two separate density arguments: for (ii) the density of polynomials in $L^2(\mu)$ forces $B(u,v_0)$ to vanish on $\supp(\mu)$ and hence $\mu$ to be the N-extremal measure on the zero set of $B$; for (iii) the disjointness of the supports of distinct N-extremal measures, together with the support identity $\eqref{eq:supp}$, forces $\mu=\mu[v_0]$. Working with N-extremal measures and indeterminate Jacobi operators in this way is well beyond ordinary PhD qualifying level.
